name: Simraungadh
tagline: The lost capital of the Karnata kings of Mithila
meta_description: Simraungadh, Bara: capital of the Karnata kings of Mithila from 1097, with earthen ramparts, the Kankali temple, Ranivas temple and Jharokhar Pokhari.
summary: Simraungadh, on the India border about 28 km east of Birgunj, was the fortified capital of the Karnata kings of Mithila from 1097 until about 1324. Today it is a Bhojpuri-speaking market town ringed by old earthen ramparts, with the Kankali temple, the Ranivas temple and a vast medieval pond. Visit for a day from Birgunj or Simara.
intro: Few travellers have heard of Simraungadh, yet for more than two centuries it was one of the most important cities of the eastern Gangetic plain. From here the Karnata kings ruled Mithila, the land between the Gandaki and Kosi rivers, and their court produced the earliest known Maithili prose. Visitors in the 13th century described a city of high walls, gates and water-filled moats. Few traces of that city stand above ground today.

Today Simraungadh is a municipality in Bara district, a flat, green farming town of about 83 metres elevation, right on the border with Bihar. The old city is mostly buried, but its outline survives as long earthen ramparts and ditches, called baahi locally, and as mounds, ponds and broken sculptures scattered through the fields. Local families still worship at the old sculptures, and ponds dug centuries ago still fill with monsoon rain.

It is a place for travellers interested in history, Hindu temples and everyday life in the Bhojpuri-speaking Terai. Combine it with Birgunj, about 28 km west, and Parsa National Park to the north. A guide who knows the sites and speaks Bhojpuri or Hindi makes the visit far richer. October to March is the comfortable season. Plan a full day and start early, as the sites are spread out and the plain is hot by midday.

story.title: Seven walls, twenty-one moats, one buried city
paras: In 1097 a commander named Nanyadeva, probably of South Indian origin, set up his own kingdom in Mithila and made Simraungadh its capital. An inscribed stone pillar dates his reign to the Saka year 1019, that is 1097 CE. His dynasty, the Karnatas, ruled Tirhut for more than two centuries, calling themselves lords of Mithila, and under them the first known work of Maithili prose, the Varna Ratnakara, was written. Simraungadh became the centre of Mithila's politics and learning.

The city was built for defence and for floods. A rectangular enclosure of earthen ramparts and ditches stretched about 7.5 km north to south. When the Tibetan monk Dharmasvamin passed in 1236 on his way home from Nalanda, he described seven tall walls, eleven large gates and 21 ditches filled with water and lined with trees. The ramparts and ditches also helped protect the city from the river floods that regularly swept the plain.

The end came with Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq's invasion of Tirhut in the 1320s. The last Karnata king, Harisimhadeva, fled north into the hills of Nepal, and his descendants married into the royal line of Bhaktapur. The city declined. Later visitors, an Italian missionary in 1740 and British officers in 1801 and the 1830s, found only ruins within a maze of walls. Much of the old city still lies unexcavated beneath the fields, divided by the modern border.

legend: Nepal's chronicles say that when Harisimhadeva fled Simraungadh ahead of the Tughlaq army, he carried with him the goddess Taleju, the protective deity of his house. She travelled into the hills with the fleeing court and later became the royal goddess of the Malla kings, enshrined in the Taleju temples of Kathmandu, Patan and Bhaktapur. Historians debate the details; devotees do not.
people: Simraungadh's people are mostly Madhesi farmers and traders who speak Bhojpuri, with Maithili and Nepali also heard. Families grow rice, wheat, sugarcane and lentils on the fertile plain, and many work across the open border in Bihar or in Birgunj. Brahmin priests, Yadav, Kushwaha, Muslim and Tharu families all live in the area.

untold.fact: The Tibetan monk Dharmasvamin passed through Simraungadh in 1236 and described a city surrounded by seven tall walls and 21 water-filled ditches, with a palace of eleven large gates.
Harisimhadeva, the last Karnata king of Simraungadh, fled to the hills of Nepal after Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq's invasion in the 1320s; his descendants are linked to the founding of the Malla dynasty.
untold.source: Wikipedia: Harisimhadeva; Wikipedia: Karnats of Mithila

untold.fact: Simraungadh's Ram Janaki temple at the Ranivas complex was built in 1878 by Jagat Jung Rana, after his father, Prime Minister Jung Bahadur Rana, died in 1877 returning from a hunt near here.

taste.name: Sattu sharbat
taste.text: Sattu, flour of roasted gram, is the backbone of Bhojpuri food. In the hot months it is whisked into cold water with lemon, salt, roasted cumin, green chilli and onion to make a cooling, filling drink. Roadside carts in Simraungadh and Kalaiya sell it from March to June.

highlights.title: Ranivas temple and palace
highlights.text: About 1 km north of the market, the Ranivas complex holds a Ram Janaki temple built in 1878 by Jagat Jung Rana. Local belief holds that it stands over the old Karnata palace. Remove shoes at the temple.

highlights.title: Kankali temple
highlights.text: A shikhara-style temple to Kankali Mai, whose black stone image is said to have been damaged by the Tughlaq army. A bell in front carries a date corresponding to 1283 CE. It is busiest at Rama Navami.

highlights.title: The earthen ramparts
highlights.text: Long banks and filled ditches, the baahi, still outline the medieval city, about 7.5 km north to south. Walking along a stretch with a guide shows the scale of the old capital. Go with a local guide.

highlights.title: Jharokhar Pokhari
highlights.text: A huge man-made pond near the border, believed to be about 800 years old. Once 52 bighas in area, it has shrunk badly, but it remains one of the largest old ponds in Nepal. Go early, while the air is cool.

highlights.title: Scattered sculptures
highlights.text: Carved stones and broken images from the Karnata period turn up in fields, under trees and in small village shrines, still worshipped by local families. Ask before touching or photographing them, as many are still worshipped.

how_to_reach.text: Simraungadh is about 28 km east of Birgunj, roughly 1 hour by car via Kalaiya. From Simara airport allow about 1.5 hours. From Kathmandu by road, drive via Hetauda and Simara, about 6 to 8 hours. Local buses and shared jeeps run from Birgunj and Kalaiya.
Fly Kathmandu to Simara (SIF), about 20 to 25 minutes, then drive about 50 km to Simraungadh. Check current status before you travel, as flight schedules change.

where_to_stay: Simraungadh has only basic lodges. Most visitors stay in Birgunj, about an hour west, which has business hotels and restaurants, or near Simara airport. A day trip from Birgunj covers the Ranivas complex, the Kankali temple, a stretch of rampart and Jharokhar Pokhari. Combine with Parsa National Park, about two hours north, for a two- or three-night trip.
tips: Hire a local guide who speaks Bhojpuri or Hindi; signage at the sites is limited.
Carry your passport; you are close to the open border with India.
Visit from October to March; April to June is extremely hot on the plains.
Dress modestly and remove shoes at temples.
Rama Navami in Chaitra (March–April) draws thousands of worshippers to the Kankali temple; expect crowds.

experiences.title: Ranivas temple and the Karnata palace site
experiences.summary: Visit the Ranivas complex north of the market, with its Ram Janaki temple built in 1878 by Jagat Jung Rana on what local belief holds is the site of the old Karnata palace. Allow one to two hours.
body: The Ranivas complex, also called the Ram Janaki temple or Mahal Sarai, stands about 1 km north of Simraungadh's market and 2 km from the Indian border. Its grounds are large, and the temple and palace buildings sit among trees and fields. Weekday mornings are usually quiet, with a few worshippers and families walking the grounds.

The present temple dates from 1878. In 1877 Jung Bahadur Rana, Nepal's powerful prime minister, died at Patharghat in Rautahat while returning from a hunting camp in the Simraungadh area. His queen, Hiranya Garbha Devi, asked before her death that a temple be built, and their son Jagat Jung Rana built it the following year. The story ties the Rana era to this corner of the Terai.

Local tradition holds that the complex stands on the ruins of the Karnata palace, and that a later Mithila king built a palace here for his daughter. Ask your guide to show you old bricks and carved stones around the site. Remove shoes at the temple and visit early before the heat. Carry water.

faqs.q: Who built the Ranivas temple in Simraungadh?
faqs.a: The present Ram Janaki temple at the Ranivas complex was built in 1878 by Jagat Jung Rana, son of Prime Minister Jung Bahadur Rana. It fulfilled the wish of Jung Bahadur's queen, Hiranya Garbha Devi, after he died in 1877 returning from a hunt in the area.

faqs.q: Is the Karnata palace still visible at Simraungadh?
faqs.a: Not as a standing building. Local tradition holds that the Ranivas complex stands on the old palace site, and old bricks and sculptures turn up around it. The clearest surviving feature of the Karnata city is its long earthen ramparts and ditches.

faqs.q: How much time do I need at the Ranivas complex?
faqs.a: One to two hours is enough to see the temple, walk the grounds and look at old stones with a guide. Combine it with the Kankali temple and Jharokhar Pokhari for a full morning in Simraungadh.

experiences.title: Kankali temple and the Tughlaq story
experiences.best_time: Morning, Oct–Mar; Rama Navami in Chaitra
experiences.summary: A shikhara-style temple in the south-east of the market, home to a black stone image of Kankali Mai said to have been damaged by the Tughlaq army, with a bell dated to the late 13th century.
body: The Kankali temple stands in the south-eastern part of Simraungadh's market area, a tall shikhara tower rising above the houses. Inside sits the black stone image of Kankali Mai, a fierce form of the goddess. Local tradition says the image was mangled by Tughlaq soldiers when the city fell in the 1320s. Families still come here to mark important moments in their lives.

Before restoration the site was simply called Kankali Mai Sthan, a ruin where people still worshipped. A sadhu named Mansaram Baba rebuilt a small temple before 1816, and the present building was raised by his disciple in 1967. A bell in front carries a date in the Lakshmana Samvat era that corresponds to 1283 CE. Ask the priest to show you the bell.

At Rama Navami in the month of Chaitra, thousands of worshippers from Nepal and India gather here. On ordinary mornings it is quiet, with a few families making offerings of flowers and vermilion. Visit respectfully, remove shoes and ask before photographing the image. Combine it with the Ranivas complex and a stretch of rampart for a full morning.

faqs.q: Who is Kankali Mai?
faqs.a: Kankali is a fierce form of the Hindu goddess, related to Kali, worshipped as a protector. At Simraungadh her black stone image is the focus of the Kankali temple, and she is an important local deity, especially during Rama Navami in Chaitra (March–April).

faqs.q: How old is the Kankali temple?
faqs.a: The present building dates from 1967, on a site restored by Mansaram Baba before 1816. The temple bell carries a date corresponding to 1283 CE, from the Karnata period, and the image is believed to be much older than the current structure.

faqs.q: Can foreigners enter the Kankali temple?
faqs.a: Respectful visitors are generally welcome in the temple grounds. Remove shoes, dress modestly and follow the lead of worshippers. Some inner areas may be reserved for Hindus; ask the priest or your guide before entering, and before taking photographs. A small offering is welcome.

experiences.title: Walk the ramparts to Jharokhar Pokhari
experiences.summary: Walk a stretch of the earthen ramparts that once enclosed the Karnata capital, through fields and villages, to Jharokhar Pokhari, a medieval man-made pond on the border believed to be about 800 years old. Start early.
body: The medieval city of Simraungadh was enclosed by earthen ramparts and ditches forming a rectangle about 7.5 km north to south and 4.5 km east to west. Locals call these banks baahi and remember the city as a labyrinth. Many stretches are now covered by fields and houses, but with a guide you can follow raised lines across the land. Ditches beside them still fill with water in the monsoon.

Your walk ends at Jharokhar Pokhari, also called Deutaal or Kachorwa Pokhari, near the Indian border. Once spread across about 52 bighas, the pond has shrunk to around 22 because of silting and encroachment, but it is still one of the largest old man-made ponds in Nepal, believed to date from the Karnata period. Birds gather on its open water in winter.

Village life fills the route: buffalo wallowing in ditches, women drying cow-dung cakes on walls, children cycling to school. Start early in the cool season, wear a hat and carry water. Keep your passport with you near the border. The walk covers a few kilometres on farm paths and village roads, flat but sunny. Bring a hat and water.

faqs.q: How big was the old city of Simraungadh?
faqs.a: The main enclosure of earthen ramparts and ditches was about 7.5 km north to south and 4.5 km east to west, and the wider fort is said to have spread over six kos. The site extends across today's border into India.

faqs.q: What is Jharokhar Pokhari?
faqs.a: Jharokhar Pokhari is a large man-made pond in Simraungadh, near the Indian border, believed to be about 800 years old. It once covered about 52 bighas but has shrunk to around 22 bighas due to poor maintenance and encroachment. It is also called Deutaal or Kachorwa Pokhari.

faqs.q: Is it safe to walk near the India border at Simraungadh?
faqs.a: Yes, the area is a normal farming landscape and the border is open for Nepali and Indian citizens. Foreign visitors must not cross into India except at official checkpoints with a valid visa. Carry your passport, stay with your guide and avoid walking after dark.

experiences.title: Bhojpuri street food in Simraungadh
experiences.image_query: Terai street food Nepal sattu litti
experiences.summary: Graze through Simraungadh's market with a local guide: sattu sharbat in the hot months, litti chokha from coal fires, jalebi, samosa and sweet milky tea, the everyday food of the Bhojpuri Terai. Go with a local guide.
body: The market of Simraungadh comes alive in the late afternoon. Carts sell sattu sharbat, roasted gram flour whisked with cold water, lemon, salt, cumin and green chilli, a drink that keeps farmers going through the heat of April and May. It is sold by the glass from carts, mixed fresh while you wait.

As evening comes, stalls light coal fires to bake litti, wheat dough stuffed with spiced sattu, served with smoky chokha of roasted aubergine, potato and tomato and a drizzle of ghee. Sweet shops fry jalebi in big pans, and tea stalls brew strong, sweet milk tea with cardamom. Snacks are cheap, so try several.

Your guide helps you choose busy, clean stalls and explains the dishes. Eat freshly cooked food, avoid raw salads and unbottled water, and carry small notes. This is cheap, filling, mostly vegetarian food. Late afternoon and early evening are the best times, when stalls are busiest and food freshest. Carry small notes and hand sanitiser.

faqs.q: What is sattu?
faqs.a: Sattu is flour made from roasted gram or other roasted grains, a staple of the Bhojpuri and Maithili plains. It is mixed into drinks, stuffed into litti, or eaten with water, salt and onion as a quick meal. It is high in protein and considered cooling in summer.

faqs.q: Is street food safe in the Terai?
faqs.a: Freshly cooked, hot food from busy stalls is generally safe. Choose places with high turnover, avoid raw salads, cut fruit and ice, and drink bottled or filtered water. Carry hand sanitiser. A local guide knows which stalls are reliable. A guide helps with communication.

faqs.q: What language is spoken in Simraungadh?
faqs.a: Bhojpuri is the main language of Simraungadh and the surrounding area, with Maithili, Hindi and Nepali also widely understood. A few words of greeting, such as pranam, are appreciated. Most shopkeepers can manage simple Hindi with visitors. Few people speak English.

faqs.q: Where is Simraungadh?
faqs.a: Simraungadh is a municipality in Bara district, Madhesh Province, on the border with Bihar. It is about 28 km east of Birgunj and 90 km south of Kathmandu as the crow flies, though the road journey from Kathmandu takes 6 to 8 hours. The nearest airport is Simara.

faqs.q: Why is Simraungadh historically important?
faqs.a: From 1097 until the 1320s it was the capital of the Karnata dynasty, which ruled Mithila. The first known work of Maithili prose was written under these kings. When the last king, Harisimhadeva, fled to Nepal's hills, his line became linked with the Malla rulers of the Kathmandu Valley.

faqs.q: What can I see in Simraungadh today?
faqs.a: The Ranivas complex with its 1878 Ram Janaki temple, the Kankali temple with a bell dated to 1283 CE, stretches of earthen ramparts and ditches from the medieval city, Jharokhar Pokhari pond and scattered old sculptures. Much of the ancient city lies buried under fields.

faqs.q: Is Simraungadh worth visiting?
faqs.a: Yes, for travellers interested in history and life in the Bhojpuri Terai. It is not a polished heritage site: there is little signage and few facilities. With a good guide, though, the ramparts, temples and stories of the Karnata kings make a rewarding day.

faqs.q: How do I get to Simraungadh?
faqs.a: Fly from Kathmandu to Simara in 20 to 25 minutes and drive about 1.5 hours, or reach Birgunj by road and drive about 1 hour east via Kalaiya. Buses and shared jeeps run from Birgunj and Kalaiya. A private car with a guide is the easiest way to see the scattered sites.

faqs.q: Who was Nanyadeva?
faqs.a: Nanyadeva founded the Karnata dynasty and made Simraungadh his capital. A stone pillar at Simraungadh dates his reign to the Saka year 1019, which is 1097 CE. He probably came from South India as a commander, and he went on to rule Mithila independently.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Simraungadh?
faqs.a: October to March, when the weather is mild. April to June brings extreme heat on the plains, often over 40 °C, and the monsoon from late June to September makes fields muddy and some sites hard to reach. December and January mornings can be foggy and cold.

faqs.q: Where should I stay when visiting Simraungadh?
faqs.a: Birgunj, about an hour west, is the best base, with business hotels and restaurants. There are also hotels near Simara airport. Simraungadh itself has only basic lodges. Plan a day trip and combine it with Parsa National Park. Book ahead in festival seasons.

faqs.q: Can I cross into India from Simraungadh?
faqs.a: The border here is open for Nepali and Indian citizens, but foreign nationals may only cross at official immigration checkpoints, such as Birgunj–Raxaul, with a valid Indian visa. Do not cross the border informally. Check current status before you travel.
